title: By my own hands
hook: a hadith: no one eats better food than what they earn with their own hands (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Amin: the merchant his town called the trustworthy. Your line was trustworthy. Which deal did you keep completely clean? Day eight hundred ninety-six.

What makes one meal taste better than another? Salt, sure. Hunger. Good company. Here's another answer, from a saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, kept in the collection of al-Bukhari. In paraphrase: no one has ever eaten better food than what they eat from the work of their own hands. And then, to make the point, he names a king. David, the prophet of God, he says, used to eat from the work of his own hands. A king, who could have had anything brought to him, earning his bread. Today's word is in that saying.
screen: `WHAT MAKES A MEAL TASTE BETTER?` → `THE WORK OF ONE'S OWN HANDS.` → `EVEN A KING.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. The saying doesn't say rich food, or holy food, or food eaten in a mosque. It says better food is what you earn yourself. The value isn't in the plate. It's in the hands that paid for it. Second, the king. The Qur'an tells of David as a prophet and a ruler, and also as a craftsman. It says God made iron soft for him and told him to make coats of mail, measuring the links with care, and to do good work. So when the hadith says David ate from the work of his hands, it points to a ruler who kept a trade. Third, the dignity in it. Another saying in al-Bukhari, in paraphrase: it's better for one of you to take a rope, bring a bundle of firewood on your back and sell it, than to go and beg from people, whether they give or refuse. Gathering firewood isn't glamorous work. The saying treats it as honorable, because it's yours. Fourth, how Muslims hold this. Earning a lawful living, halal, through honest work, is spoken of as part of faith. Muslims also give zakat, a required giving to people in need, and the hadith collections praise helping others. These sayings don't look down on anyone who receives help. They lift up the worth of honest effort, however humble. And the picture they leave is small and physical: a person sitting down to bread they paid for with their own hands, and finding it tastes good.
screen: `BETTER FOOD IS EARNED FOOD.` · `DAVID MADE COATS OF MAIL.` · `A ROPE AND A BUNDLE OF FIREWOOD.` · `HONEST EFFORT, HOWEVER HUMBLE.` · then, large: `FROM THE WORK OF HIS OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of the next thing you'll eat. Now trace it backward. Where did the money come from? Whose hours paid for it? If it's food you made yourself, picture the chopping, the stirring, the heat. If someone else's hands paid for it today, a parent, a partner, a stranger at a shelter, hold them in mind with thanks. Then look at your own hands for a breath or two, and notice what they've carried today. If you pray, you can give thanks for your food in your own tradition's words. The bell holds the time.
Al-Bukhari, whose collection keeps the saying that no one eats better food than what they earn by the work of their own hands, as David did. Today's word.
Your line: bread you paid for. Today, eat something you earned or made yourself, and eat it slowly enough to taste the work in it. Day eight hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of earning a halal, lawful living through honest work as part of faith, and teachers often cite the hadith of David eating from the work of his own hands.

original.note: Arabic, from the Islamic tradition: the work of his hand, the phrase the hadith uses for what David ate from.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saying about cooking for yourself.
what it means: food earned by your own honest work is the best food, and a prophet-king earned his.
what a scholar hears: the hadith names David, and the Qur'an pictures him as a maker of coats of mail, a ruler who kept a trade.
